chunks.text: Between roughly 1450 and 1750, large land-based empires arose across Eurasia, many expanding by mastering gunpowder weapons. Historians nickname several of them the 'gunpowder empires' because cannons and firearms were central to how they conquered.

In 1453, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II conquered Constantinople using massive bronze cannons that battered down the city's legendary triple walls. The fall ended the thousand-year Byzantine Empire and gave the Ottomans a magnificent capital, renamed Istanbul.

Gunpowder weapons shifted military advantage from defenders to attackers: heavy cannons could batter down stone city walls, and firearms let trained infantry defeat cavalry. This favored large, centralized, well-funded states that could afford expensive guns and professional soldiers.

Gunpowder helped tilt the long contest between settled empires and mobile horse nomads decisively toward the empires. Because casting cannons and maintaining gunpowder armies cost enormous sums, only powerful states with strong tax bases could field them at scale.

The gunpowder empires were not built on guns alone. Strong leadership, effective administration, religious legitimacy, and wealth from trade and taxation were all essential; gunpowder was a crucial enabler rather than the whole story.

The Ottoman Empire began around 1300 as a small frontier state of Turkic Muslim warriors in Anatolia and grew into a colossus spanning three continents: southeastern Europe (the Balkans), the Middle East, and North Africa. It was the greatest and longest-lived of the gunpowder empires.

Mehmed II was the Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 at age 21. The conquest gave the Ottomans control of the strategic straits between Europe and Asia, and Mehmed styled himself an heir to the Roman emperors.

Suleiman the Magnificent reigned over the Ottoman Empire from 1520 to 1566, the empire's zenith. His armies besieged Vienna in 1529 and expanded across the Middle East and North Africa, and his own people called him 'the Lawgiver' for reforming the legal system.

The Ottomans were Sunni Muslims, and the sultan eventually claimed the title of caliph, presenting himself as the protector of Sunni Islam. This religious identity later set them against the Shia Safavids.

The Janissaries were an elite corps of professional Ottoman infantry armed with firearms and rigorously disciplined, among the most effective troops in the world. They were recruited through the devshirme system from Christian boys of conquered Balkan villages.

The Safavid Empire was founded in 1501 by Shah Ismail, who transformed Persia (modern Iran). He established Twelver Shia Islam as the official state religion, a momentous decision since most of the surrounding Islamic world, including the Ottomans, was Sunni.

By making Shia Islam the Safavid state religion, Shah Ismail positioned the empire as the champion of Shiism against the surrounding Sunni world. This set the stage for fierce, lasting conflict with the neighboring Sunni Ottoman Empire.

Shah Abbas the Great reigned over the Safavid Empire from 1588 to 1629, its height. He reformed the army, welcomed trade, and built the magnificent capital of Isfahan, which Persians called 'half the world.'

The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526 when Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, won the Battle of Panipat against a far larger Indian army partly by using field artillery and firearms his enemies lacked.
Like the Delhi Sultanate before it, the Mughal Empire was a Muslim dynasty ruling over a Hindu-majority population in the Indian subcontinent. It ruled most of the subcontinent for two centuries.

Akbar the Great reigned over the Mughal Empire from 1556 to 1605. He expanded the empire dramatically and is most celebrated for his policy of religious tolerance toward the Hindu majority, a strategy of inclusion that helped stabilize his vast, diverse realm.

Ming China (1368–1644) and the succeeding Qing Dynasty (1644–1912, founded by the Manchus) were powerful land-based empires of the era, governed through a Confucian bureaucracy. They show that the gunpowder empires were not exclusively Islamic.
Russia was an expanding land empire of this period, growing eastward across Siberia under rulers such as Ivan IV ('the Terrible') and later the Romanovs. It was Eastern Orthodox Christian.

Tokugawa Japan was unified under the Tokugawa shogunate beginning in 1603, becoming a powerful centralized state. It is another example of a major land-based power of the early modern era beyond the Islamic empires.

Gunpowder was originally a Chinese invention that spread westward across Eurasia along the Mongol networks of the previous era. The weapon that built the early-modern land empires was itself a product of Afro-Eurasian connectivity.

In 1600, the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal empires together ruled a huge share of the world's people and wealth, and the Mughal economy was among the largest on the planet. Three of the four largest land empires of the era were Islamic, a corrective to Europe-centered narratives, since the 'rise of the West' had not yet happened.
